candidates.text: For a while my whole attention was absorbed by the just and glowing picture of infamy and avarice and more than savage cruelty held up to the Senate by the orator, and an inexpressible sympathy for the oppressed and afflicted Indians had choked my own utterance and bedimmed my vision; when, seeking relief for my fullness from the painful contemplation of dishonor and suffering, I turned my eyes across the Chamber, and lo! there sat two of the Cherokee females whom I described to you some weeks since, striving to restrain their tears, and to listen with dignified composure to the story of their wrongs. They were not always successful, for the tears would flow in spite of them. But distressed as they were—agonized as they were, I felt for the time, and so expressed myself to an acquaintance, that I would rather be those two Cherokee women, participating as they did, in the sympathies of all who heard Mr. Clay, than the two Georgia Senators, whose State he exposed to the abhorrence and detestation of the civilized world. — New-York Commercial Advertiser. A message was received from the President of the United States in relation to the execution of the enclosing the correspondence on the subject between the Secretary of War and Mr. John Ross, of the Cherokee delegation. The documents were read. The Executive offers the delegation very liberal concessions, though not all that they require, on condition that they will assent to the treaty and agree to carry it into effect. The President offers the Cherokees time, two years I believe, in which to complete the removal, provided Congress, at his recommendation, will grant it. He offers to secure to the tribe a perpetual patent for their new territory west of the Mississippi, and promised that no government shall be established over them without their consent. Mr. Clay and Mr. King of Alabama, Mr. Cuthbert and Mr. Lumpkin of Georgia and Mr. Grundy of Tennessee expressed their surprise and indignation at these papers. They had not been aware that any such negotiation was going on, and they severally and solemnly declared that the treaty should be executed forthwith; i.e. in accordance with the President's wishes.

By that agreement all the territory of the State, west of a certain line was ceded, and as a matter of condition the Indian title to lands within the then reserved limits of the State, early as practicable was to be extinguished for the use of Georgia. The Creeks and Cherokees were the only Tribes at that time within the limits of the state; and what their line and boundary of separation then was, appears to be the true point presented for considering, and settling this question. — If at that period, the boundary by both nations was supposed to be at or near the Buzzard Roost, and to run thence westwardly to Will's Creek; and that its establishment in 1821 was but the mere recognition of what before had been understood by and between the two nations, then should it be admitted, that the Cherokee claim to this disputed territory is fairly established, and the United States is placed under the necessity to protect them against intrusion upon their soil. It is not admitted, that the Creeks and Cherokees were capable to contract, so as to alter their boundary, without the consent of the other parties in interest.

FIRSTLY.— Pain cannot exist but from CORRUPT HUMORS being located in the identical part where the pain is experienced. These corrupt humors, when in sufficient quantity to overpower the principle of life, are the principal cause of death. Long continued encroachments do not indeed furnish a justification of those who make them; but they prove that the oppressors may possibly not perceive the true nature of their oppressive acts, in this matter we cannot offer even the sorry plea of prescription in crime, as an extenuation of our guilt. The precedents, in our own country, are all against us. For two hundred years the Indians have been treated like other men, as to the acknowledgment of their rights and the interpretation of treaties made with them. Cherokees are now living, who have been assured hundreds of times, by the accredited agents of our Government, that the United States would never permit any encroachment to be made upon them; that their country would remain inviolate, as long as they pleased to retain it; and that all treaties were to be executed with the strictest honor and fidelity.

At this time, to add to his embarrassment and trouble, he was threatened with removal from the office of Probate Judge in his district; an office then worth $200 to $300. Under all these circumstances, he presented his case to three distinguished members of the legislature from this county (all of them his political opponents) and with tears, begged their favor and support. Moved by pity at the narration of his afflictions and dependent circumstances, they did support him, and that too, in opposition to their own political friend, Mr. Strong, who had received the nomination in county meeting by a large majority; and, by their efforts and influence alone, he obtained the appointment. One of the members who thus supported him in his days of adversity alienated, by so doing, the favor of twenty political friends, (they knowing Mr. Phelps at that time, and predicting interference; without reproof for his course received the enviable appellation of “radical number one," which title he bore for years afterwards. The third was strongly censured for having thus sustained him. Yet gratitude, honest, heartfelt gratitude, would have been ample recompense for all this. But, sir, how did he show his gratitude for their favors? His conduct was precisely like that of the snake! not of “a snake in the grass” alone, but of the snake in the woodman's bosom!

Mr. Beck—The following “tributary sketch,” was written after the author’s removal from the “verdant banks of the Piscataqua,” The lovely spot—where childhood’s hours Passed cheerfully away. WITH joy I remember—the scene has passed; As on the Piscataqua’s banks I strayed;— The shadows of evening were falling fast, And silence’s command great Nature obeyed. When the boatman’s cry, and the dashing oars Broke soft on my ear as a magic sound; Till it died away o’er the distant shores, As the night spirit’s murmurs breathed around. The soft gentle zephyrs blew mild and clear, And the buzzing beetle began its hum; The nightingale’s song saluted my ear, And then the deep roll of the distant drum. 'Twas sweet,—as a vision it seemed to me, Where beauty and innocence held their reign; Ah! ne’er such joys again shall I see, While on Swamscut’s dark shores I must remain, SWAMSCUT BARD. The State of Georgia, despairing of ever obtaining the Cherokee country by fair and peaceable means, and being encouraged by a successful intrigue towards the Creeks, has laid claim to a portion of our territory. For our own part, we never thought that the United States in her Federal capacity would come out against the Indians in military array, and say, you must remove. She dare not do such a thing in the face of an enlightened world. But let the candid reader consider the policy, and the effects of this policy on the poor Indians, and then say that the United States are guiltless. It is her unjust measures that we complain of, and which, to our minds, partake of the nature of force. We presume our readers have not forgotten the late Creek controversy. Two Commissioners of the United States, Col. D. G. Campbell, and Maj. J. Merewether succeeded, after a previous failure, to make a fraudulent treaty with a small party of disaffected Creeks, which treaty was afterwards ratified. The Creek nation hereupon made a protest, and it was made fully apparent by them and by the Government’s agents that the treaty was obtained in a fraudulent manner, entered into by persons unauthorized on the part of the Creek nation. The illegality of the treaty was put beyond a question by its subsequent abrogation. But mark the conduct of the Government. What was her language to the poor Cherokees who had gone to the house of their father to ask that common justice may be done towards them by restoring the lands taken away from them by underhanded measures?
